item.title: The Emotion Nobody Mentions When We Talk About Money
item.description:
Shame

The Emotion Nobody Mentions When We Talk About Money

Shopping to feel better this Black Friday? Money shame may be the feeling underneath.

Posted November 27, 2026

Key points
  • More Americans are uncomfortable discussing their bank balance than their love life, politics, or religion.
  • Money shame has two forms: the inner critique and the fear of how others will judge us.
  • Research suggests shame leads people to withdraw from their finances, which can make hardship worse.
  • Empathy and connection help break the cycle.

When Anna felt low, she went shopping. Anna is a social worker I interviewed while researching financial well-being, and she told me about a particular kind of shop she was drawn to: soft fabrics, quiet music, a faint scent of something expensive. Her home and her workplace were busy and chaotic. In the shop, nothing bad could happen. Her biggest decision was which color coat to choose for spring.

The calm never lasted. It faded almost as soon as she left, and by the time the credit card bill arrived, shame and regret had taken its place.

Today is Black Friday, a day built on the promise that the right purchase will make us feel better. For many of us, as for Anna, the feeling we are trying to shop away is shame.

It is also a feeling we rarely admit to. In a 2025 Bankrate survey, 61% of U.S. adults said they were uncomfortable discussing their bank balance. Fewer felt that way about their love life (51%), their political views (24%), or their religion (18%).

Your Brain as a Forecaster

Psychologist Lisa Feldman Barrett (2017) argues that emotions are constructed by the brain rather than simply triggered. I find it helpful to think of the brain as a weather forecaster. Drawing on past experience, it constantly predicts what our bodily sensations mean, and it revises the forecast as new information comes in.

A knot in your stomach before a job interview could be hunger, dread, or excitement. Which one you feel depends partly on how your brain has learned to read situations like this one.

Many of us have years of money forecasts shaped by tension and secrecy at home. Opening a bill or splitting a restaurant check can call up an old forecast before we have even looked at the numbers. Often, that forecast is for shame.

Two Faces of Money Shame

Internal shame is the voice that says, “I’m bad with money.” It treats missing financial skills as a personal flaw, and a rare one. Everyone else seems to manage. If I struggle, it must say something about who I am.

This belief often starts early. Many of the middle-aged adults I meet, particularly women, tell me nobody talked openly about money with them when they were growing up. They learned through costly mistakes, and each mistake seemed to confirm that something was wrong with them.

External shame is about how others see us. In 1776, Adam Smith pointed out that the ancient Greeks and Romans lived comfortably without linen, yet in his own day, a respectable laborer would be ashamed to appear in public without a linen shirt. What counts as a necessity depends partly on what we need to avoid being looked down on.

Swedish researcher Bengt Starrin and colleagues (2009) tested this idea in a survey of more than 5,600 adults. Both financial stress and experiences of being shamed predicted psychosocial ill-health, and people who reported both were the most affected. Having too little money is hard, and feeling diminished because of it adds to the harm.

When Enough Should Be Enough

Money shame is not limited to poverty. It can be strongest when, by all appearances, there should be enough.

Ann-Marie is a journalist with three books to her name and steady work for well-known magazines. She is a single mother of two, widowed when her daughters were small. She still pays a large mortgage on a country house she has been unable to sell, while renting in the city near her daughters’ music schools. Her income is reasonable, but she has no buffer. One unexpected bill sets her back, and she knows what it means to stretch her last ten euros across a week of groceries.

She skips most social events because they cost money. She never mentions her worries to her daughters, which makes it hard to explain why they rarely travel or why her laptop comes along on weekends. To others, her life looks successful. She keeps the rest to herself.

Ann-Marie is far from alone. In the American Psychological Association’s Stress in America 2023 survey, 82% of adults aged 18 to 34 named money as a significant source of stress.

The Shame Spiral

Shame is a social emotion. It probably evolved to keep us in good standing with our group, but when it takes hold, it does undeniable damage. A meta-analysis of 108 studies found that shame is more strongly linked to depressive symptoms than guilt is (Kim et al., 2011).

With money, shame can also make the original problem worse. Joe Gladstone and colleagues (2021) studied this using bank records, longitudinal surveys, and comparisons of identical twins. Across six studies, people who felt financial shame were more likely to disengage from their finances. That disengagement led to poorer financial decisions, which deepened their hardship. The researchers call this a financial shame spiral, something many of us are familiar with in our daily lives.

Fear of judgment adds to the feeling of shame. In a study of middle-class consumers in debt, those who expected to be stigmatized hid their debt from friends and family, put off seeking help, and even spent more in social situations to keep up appearances (Moorhouse et al., 2023).

It’s a bit like a leak you are too embarrassed to report. The longer you hide it, the more damage it does to the house.

Loosening Shame’s Grip

The shame researcher Brené Brown (2007) describes empathy as the antidote to shame. Here are some ways to put that into practice with money.

Start with understanding rather than resolutions. Vowing to take control and cut out every bad habit rarely lasts. It helps more to ask how you got here. What did you learn about money as a child? What might your spending or avoidance have been protecting you from?

Name the feeling. When a money task makes you tense, try saying to yourself, “This is shame.” Brain-imaging research shows that putting feelings into words reduces activity in the amygdala, a region involved in emotional alarm (Lieberman et al., 2007). Naming the feeling may give your forecast a chance to update.

Remember that financial skills are learned. If you never learned them, that reflects what you were taught, and says nothing about your character. In Gladstone’s research, an intervention built around affirming acts of kindness weakened the link between shame and disengagement.

Talk to someone. In a field experiment, people who took a financial course alongside others in the same situation paid off more debt than people in the control group. Among those most afraid of judgment, learning in a group also improved well-being more than learning privately did (Moorhouse et al., 2023). A friend, a partner, or a financial counselor can all be a starting point.

For Anna, the work was learning to find calm without a new purchase. Part of that was looking a little further ahead and asking what feeling each shopping trip would leave behind. That question is worth asking today, before checkout.

item.title: Therapy Meets Leadership Coaching
item.description:
Coaching

Therapy Meets Leadership Coaching

Why therapy-enhanced coaching Is the next frontier for leadership development.

Posted November 27, 2026

Key points
  • Business acceleration and AI are increasing pressure and stress, especially on leaders and founders.
  • Traditional tools for dealing with those stressors are struggling to keep pace.
  • A more psychologically informed form of executive coaching to help leaders is emerging.

When business leaders hit a difficult patch, they have historically relied on family, business partners, mentors, and peers for emotional support and guidance. Many respond by working harder or taking practical steps, such as changing business practices; more than a few turn to prayer.

But in an era of AI and rising business pressures, even these traditional sources of support are being tested. A survey of 1,250 American business owners and senior leaders found that 60% felt more stressed than the previous year. Meanwhile, another recent poll found that 38% of executives and aspiring C-suite leaders have considered leaving their role over the last 12 months.

Boundaries? What boundaries?

Of course, it’s not just the C-suite feeling the strain. Workers report having to weather stress, uncertainty, and AI. Already eroded by email and WFH, the line between home and office has become increasingly permeable. To some extent, psychological well-being is now a workplace issue in ways it simply wasn’t a generation ago.

CEOs are experiencing the same blurring of boundaries. And some are increasingly asking, if they already need therapy in their off-hours, why not draw on its techniques while they are on-call too, as a way to sustain their performance under pressure?

But isn’t that what executive coaching is for? A 2025 survey of 90 current and former CEOs by Stanford Graduate School of Business, the Hoover Institution and The Miles Group found a majority (58%) do use a professional coach, up from 34% a decade earlier. Overall, 95% say they use either professional coaches or informal advisers to help them think through important organizational issues.

But that’s about organizational issues. What’s interesting is that senior leadership is increasingly seeking mental health support. In 2024, 85% of executive coaches surveyed by the International Coaching Federation said clients were asking for help with mental well-being. This is the new world of therapy-informed executive coaching.

Understanding real motivations and blind spots

Despite the growing openness about mental health, not everyone is keen to admit to seeing a therapist. But helping leaders understand how their personal histories, emotional patterns and relationships shape the way they lead seems a logical way to unlock deeper change.

I can confirm this is happening, as some of these executives are in my office or on Zoom with me every week. I’m not here to critique mainstream executive training or leadership development, although I do wonder whether generic leadership skills training can really prepare someone for the realities of being a CEO today. What my clients tell me they want from the approaches I’m developing with them is help navigating the pressures, relationships and personal patterns that shape how they lead.

They can access help on practical management techniques and frameworks. What’s often missing from conventional executive training is the deeper work to understand the underlying emotional and relational patterns influencing decisions and behavior.

Whether it’s a VC, a founder, or a tech leader, the aim is the same: to help them achieve “radiant change”, lasting change that comes from within, rather than applying a veneer to outward behavior. This involves a focus on the past, the present, and the future. The first step is exploring how their upbringing, family dynamics, and cultural background have shaped how they respond to conflict, relationships and pressure.

Understanding where those patterns come from helps leaders decide which serve them well and which constrain them, opening the way to a more authentic and nuanced approach to leadership. Here we begin looking at current relationships from a three-dimensional perspective, exploring what was said and felt. Understanding these patterns in slow-motion replay allows new relational skills to be built.

By looking beyond the business itself to understand themselves better, leaders can develop the self-awareness, empathy and emotional intelligence they need to lead teams, navigate conflict and build stronger stakeholder relationships.

A new face for the talking cure?

Isn’t this simply conventional therapy? I would argue not. While the approach draws on psychotherapeutic techniques, this coaching is guided by the aim of helping the client become a more effective leader.

Finally, there are cultural aspects to this trend that make me wonder if this isn’t a specifically American phenomenon. While there is interest in leaders exhibiting empathy, self-awareness, and relational intelligence, Silicon Valley’s legacy of experimentation and self-actualization may also be driving this shift.

In the late 2020s, founders are pushing beyond conventional coaching and support models of their predecessors. Many of my clients tell me they are working punishing hours to get their AI ideas to market. They recognize that their personal lives, emotional well-being and professional effectiveness are interconnected, and that addressing these connections can help them navigate the extraordinary demands they face today.

item.title: Caregiver Intel: Healing Resentment at the Holidays
item.description:
Caregiving

Caregiver Intel: Healing Resentment at the Holidays

Communicating needs and appreciating help can make the holidays happier for all.

Posted November 27, 2026

Key points
  • Plan for caregiving support in advance.
  • Make specific requests for caregiving needs.
  • Don't criticize or correct the help.
  • Remember to show appreciation for help received.

Although Phoebe was happy to live with her mother, Martha, and care for her ever since she had the stroke, there were times when she felt resentful of her two older sisters. Generally, they were supportive and grateful for Phoebe’s sacrifices and efforts. They dropped off meals now and then, and gave Phoebe little breaks here and there. But at the holidays, things were different. Unfortunately, Phoebe’s resentment usually stirred up around Thanksgiving and tended to last through the holiday season.

Traditionally for Thanksgiving, everyone gathered at her older sister Jennifer’s house, about 20 minutes from Mom’s house. Jennifer did most of the cooking, but she expected everyone to bring a side or a dessert. Phoebe struggled to care for Martha and the old house every day and would have appreciated a small holiday from chores. Instead, she juggled her usual tasks with baking a pumpkin pie and somehow managed to get Mom ready for the day.

Since the stroke, Mom had limited use of her left leg and arm and some difficulty with language, so Phoebe had to help her in and out of the car for the drive to Jennifer’s house. She would have been glad to have one of her sisters help Mom out of the car when they arrived. Instead, Jennifer and Janine watched them from the window, smiling and waving to Mom.

Once inside Jennifer’s house, Jennifer and Janine continued their preparations for the big meal. With 12 people for dinner, there was plenty to do. However, neither her sisters nor their husbands or children offered to help with Mom and give Phoebe a break. She felt like the only reason she was there was to take care of Mom. People came over to them, but it was to talk to Mom. When Mom needed help eating, no one blinked an eye. When Mom needed the bathroom, it never occurred to anyone that they should offer to take her.

Phoebe loved her big family and wanted to enjoy her time with them. But ever since Mom had the stroke and she’d moved into her house, it seemed like the family forgot about her and saw her only as Mom’s caregiver. She didn’t want another holiday to feel so terrible. She needed a plan.

When we met with Phoebe, we offered her some strategies that would likely allow her to enjoy the holidays again, while maintaining her important role as Mom’s caregiver. Perhaps you, too, will find them helpful when negotiating caregiving during the holidays.

1. Before the holiday, reach out to your family members and ask them to commit to doing a task.

First, let them know that you appreciate how busy they are with the holiday preparations. Then remind them that the holiday is important to you too and that you’d love to be able to step away from Mom to enjoy time with the rest of your family. Make the task requests specific: “Would you help her cut up her food? Would you take her to the bathroom? Would you sit with her during dessert?

2. Once you arrive on the day of the holiday, let everyone get settled.

Then gently remind your family members about what they committed to do. Tell them you appreciate their help. It will give you a chance to talk to their children and feel like part of the festivities.

3. When they do help, don’t judge how they help.

If someone cuts up Mom’s food into pieces that are too big or too small, let them work it out. If a relative isn’t quite sure how to help Mom in the bathroom, calmly explain what is needed. If they don’t do it perfectly, don’t mention it. It’s the effort they’re making to give you a little break that matters.

4. Thank them afterward for a wonderful day and also for helping make the holiday more enjoyable for you by chipping in.

A little positive reinforcement can go a long way.

item.title: "You Don't Sound Autistic to Me"
item.description:
Autism

"You Don't Sound Autistic to Me"

How a spiky profile can hide autistic strengths and weaknesses.

Posted November 27, 2026

Key points
  • Many autistic people have "spiky IQ profiles" that hide profound deficits and strengths.
  • Autism acceptance means accepting that the person that seems gifted in some areas can still require support.
  • A "spiky profile" can look very different from one autistic person to the next.
  • Autism can look very different in different people. They still require support.

Autism Spectrum Disorder has historically been diagnosed with a full psychological assessment. This assessment includes observational tests and a full Intelligence Quotient (IQ) test. Autism is often easy to see on an IQ assessment because IQ isn’t just one number. It is an assessment of a person’s strengths and weaknesses across multiple domains. The IQ number we are used to seeing is a representation of the average of many different types of aptitudes and weaknesses. Verbal comprehension, fluid reasoning, processing speed, and visual-spatial abilities are all measured with an index score that is put together to form an overall IQ score. IQ itself is a measure of averages. 100 is the average IQ. 15 is the standard deviation of the mean, so if you have an IQ above 115, you are more intelligent than 84% of the general population, and if you have an IQ of 130, you are smarter than 98% of the population.

For most neurotypicals, the IQ score is a good estimate of their ability to perform across multiple domains. It is rare for someone to have a verbal comprehension score in the 99th percentile and a working memory score in the 5th percentile. This is normal and is part of why, if you speak well, most neurotypicals assume you are intelligent across multiple domains. However, one of the hallmarks of autism that isn’t frequently discussed is what is known as a “spiky profile”. A spiky profile means that I frequently see clients with an overall IQ that is virtually meaningless because they will have verbal reasoning in the 5th percentile and be nonverbal, but have a fluid reasoning and visual spatial score in the 99th percentile, or vice versa.

This spiky profile deeply impacts how the world and the public relate to autism and autistic people. Humans in general strongly associate verbal comprehension with intelligence and aptitude, so if an autistic person’s spiky profile has profound deficits in this area, they are often labeled as level three or requiring substantial support, and if their verbal comprehension is high, no matter how profound the other deficits, they are often told they “don’t seem autistic” or denied services they may need.

I had a client a few years ago whose profile showed profound deficits in working memory and processing speed. He was unable to do basic living tasks like cleaning his room or brushing his teeth without support. Yet he was continuously told he didn’t need support and was denied support because his verbal comprehension was in the 99th percentile. Fluid reasoning is another part of IQ that people usually associate with high-functioning intelligence, and many autistic people are exceptional at spotting patterns, drawing inferences, or finding solutions to new problems and thus are assumed to be “high-functioning” or, in some cases, are told they “don’t seem” autistic.

This is the hardest part of being autistic. The spiky profile of skills and deficits is often profound in multiple areas, and people’s biases associated with aptitude and intelligence profoundly shape how much support and empathy an autistic person will get in their community at large. People think of the archetypal autistic person as being verbally awkward or less verbal, with stimming behaviors and no eye contact. But since this spiky profile is so variable in autistic people, they could have more profound deficits and be articulate and quiet and very able to mimic neurotypical social behaviors, but have a working memory that is so profoundly low that they can’t complete basic work-related or living tasks.

I found my IQ test recently. My profile is typical for an autistic person. My verbal comprehension and fluid reasoning skills are in the 99.9th percentile, but my visual-spatial reasoning skills show profound deficits, and my working memory is also slightly impaired. This, combined with an inability to read most social cues, has made my life one of hostility from most neurotypicals. People perceive me as profoundly gifted. My IQ is high, and I am very articulate. People interpret this as pretentious and often accuse me of trying to “talk down to them”, but words are my natural habitat and my vocabulary is expansive. At the same time, I am an excellent problem solver, and I can easily find solutions to problems that confound others. Yet, mental rotations are almost impossible for me, and if I am asked to think in a room with more than one conversation or to multitask, I can shut down entirely. This, combined with the fact that I honestly misread most socially complex situations and offend people while trying to be nice or behave in ways I think are helpful but people find hurtful, makes people perceive me as a jerk instead of disabled.

This can go the other way. I have clients who are perceived as having an intellectual disability when, in many domains, they are gifted. They are never given the opportunity to show their strengths because people can’t see them.

My largest handicap is interpersonal interaction, and this is very evident in my personal life. This is largely due to my inability to see anything but the best in people and my spiky intellectual profile. After seeing me in several human interactions, my son was confounded and said, “You aren’t this stupid!” He listed all my accomplishments and said I couldn’t possibly be this dumb. He wasn’t being cruel. He was only coming to terms with the fact that the mother he had seen as brilliant and unbreakable had more disabilities than he thought were possible. This is a hard thing for a child to learn. Many people struggle with this discrepancy in me, and it erodes many of my relationships. Many people see my profound deficits as purposeful negligence.

In a world where autism acceptance and awareness are needed, I believe this is the part people need to understand the most about autistic people. Our “spiky profile” creates confusion in those around us. In the early 1990s, the film Rain Man created the archetypal image of a barely verbal autistic man with limited verbal skills who was inconceivably brilliant at math. I think it is important to remember that many autistic people are like this. We can seem like the smartest person in the room and at the same time be the most incapable person in the room

item.title: What Darwin’s Bees Tell Us About Right and Wrong
item.description:
Ethics and Morality

What Darwin’s Bees Tell Us About Right and Wrong

From Protagoras to Hume to Darwin: The origins of morality

Posted November 27, 2026

Key points
  • Models show how morality could evolve, but empirical evidence remains a key gap.
  • Which moral attitudes are inherited and which are culturally acquired remains unresolved.
  • Darwin’s bees suggest moral intuitions depend on a species’ social conditions, not universal rules.

Evolutionary explanations of morality have been of scientific interest since at least Darwin. Proto-Darwinian explanations, however, have been around for much longer. The attempt to explain morality has a long tradition going back as far as ancient Greece.

This is why I’ve recently published an academic article on the topic.

What Darwin's Bees Tell Us About Right and Wrong
Source: Robert So / Pexels

A myth and a sketch

Protagoras, in one of Plato’s dialogues, provides perhaps the first scientific explanation of morality as a set of norms and enforcement agencies, an invention of humanity to escape a Hobbesian state of nature. Couched in terms of a myth, we may treat this as a mere just-so story.

Much later, David Hume came astonishingly close to providing a Darwinian explanation of morality himself. Rainer Hegselmann and Oliver Will identify four key components of Hume’s account: a pre-societal human nature with confined generosity, the invention of artificial values to be reinforced and internalized through the approval and disapproval of others, a division of labor reaping the benefits of cooperation and trust, and the invention of central authorities that monitor, enforce, and eventually punish behavior.

These accounts, a mere story and myth in the case of Protagoras and an informal suggestion of a how-possibly explanation in the case of Hume, leave much to be desired, but they were nevertheless the best explanations available at the time.

Darwin’s hive-bees

Luckily, it did not take two millennia for the next advancement. Less than a century after Hume’s death, Darwin delivered the means for pushing the inquiry into human morality further, filling a gap Hume could only describe as nature.

Darwin himself suggested that the origin of morality can be explained with his theory. He did not maintain that any social animal, if its intellectual faculties were to become as highly developed as ours, would acquire exactly the same moral sense. If, to take his extreme case, humans were reared under precisely the same conditions as hive-bees, our unmarried females would, like the worker-bees, “think it a sacred duty to kill their brothers.” Mothers would strive to kill their fertile daughters, and no one would think of interfering. Nevertheless, the bee, or any other social animal, would gain, as it appeared to Darwin, some feeling of right or wrong, or a conscience.

The thought is unsettling. What a creature feels to be right and wrong depends on the kind of creature it is and the conditions under which it lives.

From stories to models

This, of course, is still “just” a how-possibly explanation, or, as critics like to call them, a just-so story. It should be clear, however, that from Protagoras over to Hume to Darwin, significant improvements in the explanation of morality have been made, with more and more gaps being closed. Explanations come in degrees, and this research program is providing better and better explanations.

article continues after advertisement

Unfortunately, it took a while until informal evolutionary explanations resting on the good of the species were replaced with formal models from evolutionary game theory, showing that the origin of moral behavior is not much of a mystery after all. The philosopher Brian Skyrms was the first to apply evolutionary game theory to unpack Hume’s account in a formal manner, with others following in the creation of new models and simulations.

These sets of models strengthen our confidence that morality could have evolved in a way envisioned by Hume and Darwin, providing considerable explanatory power, even though empirical work has, hitherto, been largely left out of the picture.

An old tradition with new tools

Modelers such as Skyrms simply continue an old philosophical school of thought with the modern tools of science, a move that ought to be encouraged. Even the work of moral philosophers in this Humean tradition has been very empirical and guided by science, trying to unpack the idea of morality being a mere artifact. It is a case in point for the division of labor between philosophers, modelers, and empirical researchers.

Akin to other primates, evolution equipped us with emotions and other cognitive machinery in order to solve interdependent decision problems. We do not know yet which of our moral attitudes are hard-wired and which are culturally acquired, but that is obviously no reason not to ask the question. Darwin’s bees tell us what kind of answer to expect: one that depends on the problems of living together that a species has to solve.

item.title: What We Are Bound To Lose in an Optimized Future
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

What We Are Bound To Lose in an Optimized Future

How meaningful challenges fuel psychological growth.

Posted November 27, 2026

Flow needs friction. Challenges are not the opposite of joy, but a necessary counterpart of our most beautiful journeys.
Source: Walther. ChatGTP. 2026

December invites a peculiar ritual. We look back at the year, count our achievements, contemplate our disappointments, and begin constructing a better version of ourselves for January. In 2026, artificial intelligence became an increasingly available accomplice in this exercise. It can summarize our accomplishments, identify inefficiencies, suggest resolutions, and construct an impressively optimized roadmap for 2027. Yet imagine reviewing your year differently. Instead of asking what went according to plan, consider what happened because it didn't. The conversation you never intended to have. The problem that refused to disappear. The project that demanded more than you thought you could give. Perhaps the moments that changed you most were precisely those that resisted optimization.

This possibility deserves attention as we enter another year of accelerating algorithmic assistance. We have become extraordinarily good at eliminating inconvenience, yet psychological flourishing may depend partly on experiences that cannot be anticipated, accelerated, or outsourced. The interplay between friction and flow offers a way to understand why.

The strange value of what resists us

We generally prefer ease, but our relationship with effort is more complicated than this preference suggests. A 2024 meta-analysis in Psychological Bulletin confirmed that mental effort is commonly experienced as unpleasant. Yet research published in Cognition in 2025, drawing on six studies involving 2,883 participants, found that exerting effort can increase an activity's perceived meaningfulness. One experiment compared writing with and without ChatGPT assistance. Greater effort contributed to meaning only up to a point. Still, the findings illuminate something that efficiency calculations routinely overlook. We may dislike the difficulty of an experience while valuing what that difficulty allows us to become. This paradox helps explain why flow, the state of intense absorption described by Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi, cannot simply be manufactured by making everything easier.

A meta-analysis examining the relationship between challenge and skill found that their balance contributes significantly to flow, alongside clear goals and a sense of control. More recent research in Communications Psychology emphasizes autonomy and the personal significance of an activity. Flow emerges through engagement with something sufficiently demanding to absorb us, yet manageable enough to sustain participation. The pianist needs a piece that stretches her abilities; the writer needs an idea that refuses to settle into easy sentences. Friction provides the resistance through which skill becomes experience, and experience becomes satisfaction.

Now consider an algorithmic environment increasingly designed to anticipate our desires and remove obstacles before we encounter them. Recommendations narrow our search; predictive systems streamline our choices, and generative AI can produce results without requiring us to navigate the uncertainties of creation. Such assistance can be enormously beneficial, particularly when it relieves unnecessary burdens. Yet when friction disappears indiscriminately, we risk losing opportunities for the very engagement that makes flow possible. A life engineered for effortless outcomes might become strangely impoverished in the experiences through which we develop competence, confidence, and curiosity. This remains a psychological risk rather than an established destiny, but it raises an essential question: Are we optimizing the quality of our experiences, or merely the speed with which we move through them?

A richer way to measure a year

Research suggests that our conventional understanding of a good life may itself be incomplete. Some consider psychological richness a dimension of well-being alongside happiness and meaning. A related 2025 review in Trends in Cognitive Sciences describes psychologically rich lives as those containing diverse, interesting, and perspective-changing experiences. To be clear, such experiences are not uniformly pleasant. An unfamiliar place, a challenging encounter, or an unexpected reversal may enlarge our understanding precisely because it disrupts familiar assumptions. This opens an interesting perspective on December's customary stocktaking.

The experiences that made 2026 psychologically rich may be poorly represented by our conventional measures of success. A friendship deepened through disagreement, an unexpected professional change, or an abandoned plan that opened an unforeseen possibility might have contributed more to personal development than another efficiently completed task. Of course, hardship is not inherently beneficial. Financial insecurity, discrimination, illness, and exhausting administrative obstacles can diminish well-being and restrict agency. The distinction worth preserving is between friction that erodes our ability to flourish and friction that invites us to exercise it.

The approaching new year makes this distinction painfully relevant. Research on the fresh start effect shows that temporal landmarks, including the beginning of a new year, can motivate humans to pursue aspirations. Perhaps we could use this psychological opening differently in December 2026? Rather than designing another year around the elimination of effort, we might ask which forms of friction deserve a place in our lives. Which difficulties strengthen our abilities? Which uncertainties invite discovery? Which activities would lose their meaning if someone—or something—completed them for us?

BLISS: A different resolution for 2027

The challenge is to choose meaningful friction deliberately, without turning everyday life into an obstacle course. BLISS offers five practical ways to cultivate that judgment.

B — Begin before borrowing. Give your own imagination an opportunity to work before requesting an algorithmic solution.

L — Let learning take time. Preserve activities in which gradual improvement brings satisfaction, even when shortcuts are readily available.

I — Invite the unfamiliar. Explore beyond personalized recommendations; seek perspectives and experiences that might challenge established preferences.

S — Stay with the struggle. When a difficulty is productive, resist the urge to eliminate it immediately. Allow yourself the satisfaction of finding a way through.

S — Save space for surprise. Leave some time unplanned, some questions unanswered, and some possibilities unexplored until they present themselves.

We can welcome intelligent technologies that reduce unnecessary suffering while protecting the experiences that develop natural intelligence. An increasingly capable algorithmic future need not become a frictionless one, provided we retain the freedom and capacity to choose where human effort matters. As 2026 ends, perhaps the most meaningful resolution for 2027 is not to become more efficient, organized, or productive. It is to become more attentive to what makes life worth living. The winding path through unfamiliar territory may take longer, demand more, and occasionally lead somewhere unexpected. Yet it may also reveal capacities and possibilities that a perfectly optimized route would never allow us to discover.

We need friction to find flow. And sometimes, the detour is the destination.

item.title: What Elizabeth Holmes's Stare Doesn’t Say
item.description:
Body Language

What Elizabeth Holmes's Stare Doesn’t Say

The science behind blinking, lying, and snap judgments.

Posted November 27, 2026

Key points
  • Adults blink about 14 to 17 times a minute, and the rate drops when the mind is working hard.
  • People tend to blink less while lying and more right afterward.
  • An unblinking stare is not a sign of psychopathy.

In Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s documentary You Can See Everything, the camera cuts to a tight close-up of the upper half of Elizabeth Holmes’s face. Her large blue eyes hold Fielder’s gaze for an extraordinarily long time without blinking. It was quite distracting. I found myself counting the seconds between blinks and trying to match them. I couldn’t keep up.

Holmes’s partner, Billy Evans, has the same wide blue eyes and unblinking gaze. It was unnerving to watch them even in the safety of my own living room.

But why?

Why We Blink

Blinking is a coordinated sensorimotor action that protects the eyes while reflecting shifts in attention and cognitive load. Adults typically blink about 14 to 17 times per minute, with each blink lasting roughly 100 to 300 milliseconds.

People naturally blink less when they’re working hard to focus. Studies in cognitive and auditory neuroscience show that people systematically blink less during moments of high cognitive demand. For example, people blink less in noisy environments so they don’t miss visual cues like lip movement.

Holmes and Evans don’t just blink less; their wide-eyed look shows white around the iris. This effect comes from how far the eyelids open, not how often they close. Put the two together—wide-open lids and a low blink rate—and you get a jarring laser-focused stare. The iris, an orb floating in a white sea of sclera.

Research by Tamami Nakano found that people watching someone speak tend to sync their blinks with the speaker's. When I tried to match Holmes's blinks and failed, I was consciously doing what viewers do without noticing.

Blinking and Honesty

Psychologists Sharon Leal and Aldert Vrij found that people blinked less when they lied and blinked more than usual right afterward. Their 2008 research concluded that lying is cognitively demanding. Blinking slows while the lie is being told, then rebounds once it's over.

I’m not suggesting Holmes is a liar. Someone who blinks less might be lying, but they may also be concentrating, self-conscious in front of a camera, on medication, or simply a person who blinks less than average. A low blink rate, in and of itself, suggests someone may be working hard. It doesn’t tell us at what.

The Psychopathic Stare

Holmes’s stare also reminded me of Anthony Hopkins’s Oscar-winning performance as Hannibal Lecter in The Silence of the Lambs. Hopkins said in an interview that he deliberately minimized blinking while playing the cannibalistic serial killer. The result was an unflinching performance that made Lecter feel oddly calm, predatory, and menacing.

While popular culture associates unblinking stares with sociopathy, the research doesn’t support it. In fact, some studies suggest that people high in psychopathic traits pay less attention to other people’s eyes, not more. An unblinking stare is not a reliable indicator of a personality disorder. It can be an effective tool for an actor or for a young founder delivering a TEDMED talk, as Holmes did in 2014. But it’s not diagnostic.

Snap Judgments

In the 2005 bestseller Blink: The Power of Thinking Without Thinking, author Malcolm Gladwell argued that snap judgments and first impressions formed within the first two seconds can be just as accurate as slow, deliberate analysis. “There can be as much value in the blink of an eye as in months of rational analysis,” he wrote.

Gladwell wasn’t writing about literal blinking, but he attached a condition that matters here: fast judgments are trustworthy only when they’re grounded in real experience.

My first reaction to Holmes and Evans was a snap judgment. I don’t have any real expertise in reading blink rates. What I have is a cultural script (Hannibal Lecter, the wide-eyed villain) and an expectation about conversational rhythm, which includes blinking and looking away occasionally.

That doesn’t make my unease any less valid. It was real information about me. It told me that Holmes’s stare had broken a social rhythm, and that I was primed to read that break as menace.

The documentary title promises we can see everything. The close-up on Holmes’s eyes reminds us we can’t. All we can see is that she isn’t blinking. We can’t see why.

item.title: Why You’re Stressed When Everyone Else Seems Fine
item.description:
Stress

Why You’re Stressed When Everyone Else Seems Fine

Your stress response is shaped by both the event and what the event means to you

Posted November 27, 2026

You have to start your report, but you can't log into your email.

You type your password carefully.

Wrong.

Try again.

Wrong again.

Maybe the third time is the charm.

Now your account is locked for 24 hours!

You slam the laptop shut, fighting the urge to scream profanities into the void.

Later that day, you remember how calmly your friend reacted when their computer died; they lost not only work but personal photos, videos, and much more. How could something so small stress one person out while something more serious barely affects another? For some people, a messy home is stressful. For others, waiting in line at the bank, being around screaming kids, or Christmas shopping. Stress depends not only on what happens, but on what we think it means, and whether we believe we have the resources to deal with it.

Or, according to an acquaintance of mine, pretty much every day at the office.

Lazarus and Folkman’s transactional model suggests that our different reactions to stressors may come down to primary and secondary appraisal. Primary appraisal involves assessing whether an event matters to us and whether it represents harm, loss, threat, or challenge. Secondary appraisal involves assessing whether we have the resources and options to cope with it. An event can threaten anything that matters to us, be it our health, self-esteem, values, commitments, or goals.

The science of why different things stress different people

The situation itself influences the appraisal process: how we interpret it, and the resources we believe we have.

  1. What is the event like?

The situation itself: Two people might react very differently to the same situation, yet a closer look shows they aren't really in the same situation. Consider romantic breakups. One person may move on quickly, while another may struggle with the emotional consequences for years. What makes some breakups more stressful than others?

Research suggests that events tend to be more stressful when they are sudden, severe, ambiguous, uncontrollable, or long-lasting. For instance, a sudden, unexpected breakup may be different from a mutual breakup that follows a gradual deterioration in the relationship.

  1. What does the event mean to you?

Our individual characteristics also influence how we perceive and interpret an event. Namely, personality factors such as higher levels of neuroticism and greater intolerance of uncertainty have been associated with greater stress and distress.

Our values, commitments, and goals also shape how we interpret an event.

Someone who has always imagined a future of marriage and children might experience a potential breakup as a threat not only to their immediate relationship needs, but also to their future and their sense of self. Another person whose identity and goals are strongly focused on career advancement might experience the breakup differently.

  1. What resources do you believe you have?

There are different types of resources. Internal resources include skills, experience, physical and mental health, and a sense of agency and control. External resources include practical assistance, social support, money, access to information, and professional help.

What matters for stress is not just whether these resources exist, but whether we perceive them as available and sufficient to help us cope. For example, someone may have supportive friends or family but not feel comfortable confiding in them (or assume they can't help much). Our appraisal of available resources can influence how threatening or manageable an event feels.

Therefore, a breakup may be more challenging for someone who is socially isolated, dealing with financial difficulties, has limited access to mental health services, or lacks confidence in their ability to cope effectively.

Takeaway

The next time you're wondering why something is stressing you, ask yourself three questions:

1. What actually happened?

Consider event characteristics, such as suddenness, severity, uncertainty, controllability, and duration.

2. What's at stake for me?

Some threats may be obvious, such as those involving your safety, health, or finances. But a situation can also threaten your goals, values, self-esteem, relationships, or sense of identity.

3. Do I believe I can handle it?

Your confidence in your ability to handle it matters; internal and external resources can influence this, including experience, knowledge, social support, health, practical resources, perceived control, and coping skills.

One final point: comparing your stress response with someone else's can be misleading. We can observe how other people react to events, but we cannot know exactly how they perceive or interpret those events. Just because you experienced more stress than someone else does not mean you are less resilient.

Resilience is not the same as stress reactivity. It is about adapting successfully to adversity, not about feeling stress in the first place. A strong stress response is not a judgment on your character. It just says what happened really mattered to you.

item.title: How to Know When It’s Time to End Therapy
item.description:
Therapy

How to Know When It’s Time to End Therapy

A therapist's response to concerns can tell you a lot about the relationship.

Posted November 27, 2026

Key points
  • Questioning your therapist can be an opportunity to talk about your goals and how therapy is going.
  • Research shows clients tend to do better when therapists acknowledge and repair ruptures in the relationship.
  • When a client decides to end therapy, the therapist is responsible for supporting that decision.
Source: Zeki Okur / Unsplash

"Got it. Best wishes for your continued personal development and your career.”

That was the message I received from my therapist of two years after I sent him a thoughtful email to terminate our work together.

After our last session didn’t go well, I questioned whether I wanted a termination session. Something inside me told me it was the last time I’d see him. I had brought up something he had done that didn’t feel good and had reenacted a feeling of abandonment.

After I left, I remember thinking, “He didn’t handle that well.”

I realize now that the part of me that didn’t want to have a final termination session in person had intuitively sensed his response. His email confirmed what I had felt, and I realized I was protecting myself from having to experience his coldness in person.

Being a therapist who is also looking for a therapist has given me a deeper appreciation for how important the therapeutic relationship is.

Shortly after, I consulted with another therapist. When he asked about my past therapy, I told him how it had ended. Rather than acknowledge how it might have felt to receive that response from a therapist I’d worked with for two years, he said he could understand my therapist’s response because “maybe he still had more work to do with me.”

Maybe he had more work to do with me, I thought, confused. It was my therapy, not my therapist’s. I was making a decision about what was best for me.

When clients are brave enough to recognize when something isn’t working and communicate that to their therapist, they may still question themselves, especially if they grew up in families where their feelings and needs weren’t acknowledged.

There were many times when I thought about terminating with my therapist, and a few times when I consulted with other therapists during our work together. I’ve come to recognize a pattern of staying in situations and relationships longer than I want to or should.

I think many of us have a hard time knowing when to end relationships, including our therapeutic relationships. We may question whether we’re being too sensitive, whether we’re expecting too much, or whether something that didn’t feel good was our own issue to work through.

If you’re in therapy and questioning whether you’re with the right therapist, it doesn’t automatically mean you’re not. It could be an opportunity for you and your therapist to check in about your goals and how things are going. I had done that with my own therapist, too. More than once, I told him I had a desire for him to pursue me more and ask questions about my past, but he didn’t seem to understand what I was trying to communicate. That was part of what contributed to my decision to leave.

Clients should be able to bring all of themselves into therapy and say how they feel, even when what they say might feel personal to the therapist. That’s part of our work as therapists. We have to be willing to examine our own reactions and understand how our expectations and unresolved feelings can influence the therapeutic relationship. In clinical terms, it’s working with transference and countertransference.

Our clients’ therapy is about them, not us.

Yes, therapy is a relationship, and we are part of that relationship. But when we aren’t aware of our own reactions, we can perpetuate the very wounds our clients are trying to repair.

Research supports the importance of paying attention to the therapeutic relationship, particularly when something goes wrong. A 2018 meta-analysis by Catherine Eubanks, J. Christopher Muran, and Jeremy Safran found a moderate association between successful rupture repair and positive psychotherapy outcomes.

The American Psychological Association also emphasizes that therapists should respond to signs of a rupture without becoming defensive, acknowledge their own contributions when appropriate, and examine their emotional reactions through self-awareness, consultation, and supervision.

A rupture doesn’t automatically mean therapy should end. Sometimes working through a difficult interaction can become an important part of the work. But repair requires a therapist who is willing to listen, take responsibility, and understand the impact of their behavior. Clients shouldn’t have to convince their therapist that their experience matters.

Therapy can offer us a reparative experience with endings. Many of us don’t know how to end relationships well. We may avoid difficult conversations, stay longer than we want, or leave without expressing what we feel. A thoughtful termination gives us an opportunity to reflect on the relationship, acknowledge what we’ve gained, express what didn’t work, and say goodbye.

For some clients, having a therapist who can make room for those conversations can be an important part of their healing.

When clients choose to end therapy, it’s our responsibility to support their decisions, even when we have our own feelings about the ending. A therapist might feel disappointed, sad, or hurt. Those feelings deserve attention, but they’re the therapist’s responsibility to work through, not the client’s.

If a therapist believes a client would benefit from another session or a different kind of ending, they can express that and invite a conversation. They also have to respect the client’s choice.

If you find yourself looking for another therapist while still working with your current one, it may be worth asking why. If you consistently feel missed, misunderstood, or as though your therapist is making assumptions about your experience, those are things worth bringing into the room. They may become important areas of exploration.

But if you can’t raise your concerns without offending your therapist, or repeated attempts to communicate what you need don’t lead to greater understanding, it may be time to consider ending the relationship.

You don’t need your therapist’s permission to end therapy or to prove your reasons are good enough. Therapy can help you develop a stronger relationship with yourself, including the ability to recognize when something isn’t working and make decisions that support your well-being.

Sometimes trusting yourself to know when to leave is part of the work.
